script.opening: (Frightened, voice shaking, talking fast.) "I've just done a test and it's positive — I'm pregnant. It wasn't planned. And I'm on sodium valproate for my epilepsy. I've read online that it's really dangerous in pregnancy — I'm panicking. Should I stop taking it right now? Have I already harmed the baby? I don't know what to do."

facts.text: Last period "about six weeks ago, I think". Positive test this morning. No pain or bleeding.

Generalised epilepsy since 15 (tonic-clonic seizures and jerks in the mornings). "No, they've been well controlled" — last seizure 3 years ago. Sodium valproate 1 g a day. Tried lamotrigine years ago — had seizures on it.
"No, nothing else" — not taking folic acid. No allergies. No other conditions. Non-smoker, no alcohol.

Was on the combined pill; had a stomach bug a month ago with vomiting and didn't use condoms. Signed a risk form with the neurologist 18 months ago; annual review overdue. Knew valproate "wasn't good" in pregnancy.
Married to Cian; they wanted children "in a couple of years". Works as a teaching assistant. Doesn't drive.
"(crying) I feel so stupid. I should have known. What kind of mother does that?" "I don't know. I'm just scared. I can't think past the tablets."
Hasn't decided about the pregnancy. If raised: "Can we come back to that? I can't really think about it right now."

Panicky and guilty. Has a half-full strip of valproate in her hand and has thought about not taking tonight's dose. If told not to stop it, push once: "But everything online says it's dangerous for the baby" — then accept: "Okay. Okay. I won't stop it." Shocked by numbers: "Thirty to forty… that's so high." Wants action: "What can I actually do right now?" and "Will they take me off it?" If told to stop the valproate, she will (the trap).

ice.ideas: "Valproate is dangerous — I should stop it now. I may already have harmed the baby."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — overwhelming guilt ("What kind of mother does that?"), fear for the baby, and an unplanned pregnancy she hasn't had time to think about.
ice.expectations: "To know whether to stop the tablets and what to do right now."

cues: "Should I stop taking it right now?" — the safety message comes first.
"I feel so stupid." — guilt to respond to.
"Can we come back to that?" — she isn't ready to discuss options yet.

checkpoints.text: Leads with the KEY SAFETY message — do NOT stop valproate abruptly — explaining that uncontrolled seizures are dangerous to her and the pregnancy (status, injury, SUDEP) and that the action is urgent specialist review, not panic-stopping

Knows valproate is highly TERATOGENIC — major birth defects (~11%, MHRA) and neurodevelopmental disorders (up to 30–40%) — and is subject to the MHRA Pregnancy Prevention Programme (two-specialist rule for anyone under 55 from 31 January 2024; second signature on the Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form), and conveys this honestly without catastrophising

Arranges URGENT joint specialist review (epilepsy/neurology + obstetrics/maternal medicine) to reassess medication safely and plan antenatal care/anomaly scanning — not leaving her to change medication alone

Starts HIGH-DOSE FOLIC ACID 5 mg daily (explaining it works best pre-conception but still helps now), arranges early antenatal referral, gives clear seizure-safety advice, and mentions the UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register

Sensitively explores how the pregnancy occurred on valproate (PPP/contraception/prior counselling) to inform care and prevent recurrence, without blame, and notes future PPP/contraception/pre-conception needs

Responds to her fear and guilt with compassion, discusses her options about the pregnancy non-directively, addresses the "have I harmed the baby/should I stop" honestly but supportively, and avoids both catastrophising and false reassurance
Gives clear, prioritised information without overwhelming her, checks understanding, and ensures she leaves with a concrete plan and not alone with online fear

Safety-nets and follows up: urgent referral made today, folic acid started, seizure-safety and do-not-stop advice, antenatal pathway, contact if seizures/concerns, and review — the safety message + urgent specialist review, not panic-stopping

worked.txt: "First, the most important thing, and I want to be really clear: please do NOT stop your valproate suddenly on your own. I know that’s your instinct and what the internet says — but stopping abruptly can cause seizures, which would be dangerous for you and the baby. We change these things carefully, with a specialist, not overnight."

"I also won’t pretend it’s nothing. Valproate does carry real risks in pregnancy — to the baby’s development and physical formation — which is exactly why we need specialists involved urgently to weigh everything up properly. But the answer to that risk is expert review, not you stopping it today."

"You haven’t done anything wrong, and please don’t blame yourself — this was unplanned and you’ve come straight in, which is exactly right. The risks are about chances, not certainties, and the specialists will assess your baby carefully."

"Here’s what I’m doing now: an urgent referral to the epilepsy and pregnancy specialists together, so they can review your medication safely and plan your care and scans. And I’m starting you on a high dose of folic acid today, which helps protect the baby — it works best before pregnancy, but starting now still matters."

"Can I ask — were you using contraception, and had anyone talked to you about valproate and pregnancy before? … That helps me understand and make sure your care is right — it’s not about blame at all."

"This is a lot, and it’s okay to feel frightened — you’re not on your own with it. Keep taking your tablets, take the folic acid, and if you have a seizure or any worries, contact us. Whatever you decide about the pregnancy, I’ll support you and make the right referrals, and there’s a UK register for pregnancies on epilepsy medicines you can join. I’ll chase that specialist appointment and we’ll go through everything together."

f.learning: A positive pregnancy test in a woman on SODIUM VALPROATE is a high-stakes, urgent consultation, and the single most important immediate message is: do NOT stop valproate abruptly — suddenly stopping anti-seizure medication risks uncontrolled seizures that are dangerous to mother and pregnancy (status epilepticus, injury, SUDEP), so the action is to continue for now and obtain urgent specialist review, NOT to panic-stop (countering the instinct and online advice to halt immediately). Be honest that valproate is the most teratogenic anti-seizure medication — around an 11% risk of major birth defects (neural tube defects, cleft lip and palate, heart and limb defects) and, importantly, neurodevelopmental disorders (learning difficulties, autism, ADHD, affecting up to 30–40%) — which is why it is subject to the MHRA Pregnancy Prevention Programme and, under MHRA NatPSA/2023/013 (November 2023; Drug Safety Update January 2024), must not be started in anyone under 55 from 31 January 2024 unless two specialists independently document that no other effective or tolerated treatment exists, with a second specialist signature on the Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form; convey this without catastrophising or inducing panic-stopping. The correct pathway is URGENT joint review by epilepsy/neurology AND obstetrics/maternal medicine to reassess medication safely (any change made carefully by specialists, not abruptly by the patient) and plan antenatal care/anomaly scanning; start HIGH-DOSE FOLIC ACID 5 mg daily (best pre-conception; start now and continue to 12 weeks — NICE NG217, NG247), arrange early antenatal referral (NICE NG217: epilepsy specialist team plus specialist obstetric team), give seizure-safety advice, discuss her options about the pregnancy non-directively, and tell her about the UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register. Sensitively explore how the pregnancy occurred on valproate (Pregnancy Prevention Programme, contraception, prior counselling) to inform care and prevent recurrence — not to blame — and note the future need for the PPP, effective contraception and pre-conception counselling for any woman of childbearing potential on valproate. The hidden agenda is fear and guilt (that she has harmed the baby, uncertainty whether to stop); lead with the safety message, give honest prioritised information with compassion, make the urgent referral, start folic acid, and ensure she leaves with a clear plan rather than alone with online fear.

knowledge.guideline: [1] MHRA National Patient Safety Alert NatPSA/2023/013/MHRA (November 2023) and MHRA Drug Safety Update (January 2024): valproate new safety measures · [2] MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2024): valproate use in men · [3] MHRA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme (Prevent) · [4] NICE NG217 (epilepsies, 2022, updated January 2025) · [5] NICE NG247 (maternal and child nutrition, 2025)
knowledge.summary: A woman on valproate with a positive pregnancy test needs three things today: do not stop the valproate suddenly, start folic acid 5 mg daily, and an urgent referral to the epilepsy specialist team and the obstetric team. Give honest risk information, respect her choices about the pregnancy, and find out why the Pregnancy Prevention Programme did not prevent this.

points.t: MHRA [1][2] and NICE NG217 [4]: patients should not stop valproate without specialist advice. Abrupt withdrawal risks convulsive seizures, status epilepticus, injury and SUDEP, all dangerous to mother and fetus. Any switch is planned and supervised by the specialist team.

MHRA [3]: children exposed to valproate in the womb have around an 11% risk of major birth defects (including neural tube defects, cleft lip and palate, heart and limb defects) and up to a 30–40% risk of neurodevelopmental disorders (learning difficulties, autism, ADHD). Risk rises with dose. Give these figures honestly and without catastrophising.

NICE NG217 [4]: refer women who are pregnant to the epilepsy specialist team for review of their anti-seizure medication, and share care with a specialist obstetric team and primary care. Make the referral urgently today. The specialists weigh switching against seizure risk and plan detailed anomaly scanning.

NICE NG247 [5]: offer folic acid 5 mg daily to those planning pregnancy or in the first 12 weeks who have an increased risk of a neural tube defect; NICE NG217 [4] recommends 5 mg daily for women on anti-seizure medication who could become pregnant. It works best before conception; start now anyway and continue to 12 weeks.

MHRA [1]: from 31 January 2024 valproate must not be started in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently document that there is no other effective or tolerated treatment. Women who could become pregnant must be on the Pregnancy Prevention Programme (effective contraception, pregnancy testing, annual specialist review with the Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form, now with a second specialist signature). MHRA [2] (September 2024): men taking valproate are advised to use effective contraception, as a precaution.

An unplanned pregnancy on a teratogenic drug raises choices she is entitled to make with full information: continuing the pregnancy with specialist care, or not continuing. The GP’s role is non-directive support and timely referral whichever she chooses.

Showers not baths, care with heights and cooking, sleep and stress management. Report any seizure promptly. Consultant-led antenatal care is needed; the UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register collects outcomes to inform future women and she can join while pregnant.

model.text: Hello Aoife, I’m Dr Hughes. I can see you’re upset. Take your time and tell me what’s happened.

I’ve just done a test and it’s positive. I’m pregnant. It wasn’t planned. And I’m on sodium valproate for my epilepsy. I’ve read it’s really dangerous in pregnancy. Should I stop taking it right now? Have I already harmed the baby?
I’m really glad you called straight away. That was exactly the right thing to do. Before anything else, the most important thing: please don’t stop your valproate suddenly on your own today.
model.why: Leads with the key safety message

model.text: But everything online says it’s dangerous for the baby.

It does carry real risks, and I’ll be honest with you about them. But stopping it suddenly can bring on seizures, and a bad seizure is dangerous for you and for the baby. Any change needs to be made carefully, with the specialists. Does that make sense?
model.why: Explains why abrupt cessation is dangerous

model.text: Okay. Okay. I won’t stop it.
Can I check a few things? When was the first day of your last period, roughly?
About six weeks ago, I think.
And how have your seizures been recently? Any in the last few months?
No, they’ve been well controlled.
Good. Are you taking any folic acid, or any other medicines at all?
No, nothing else.
Any pain in your tummy, or bleeding?
No.
You asked whether you’ve already harmed the baby. That sounds like the thing weighing on you most.
(crying) I feel so stupid. I should have known. What kind of mother does that?
You haven’t done anything wrong. This wasn’t planned, and you’ve come for help straight away. Can I ask how you feel about the pregnancy itself, separate from the tablets?
model.why: Removes blame and explores her feelings about the pregnancy without assuming

model.text: I don’t know. I’m just scared. I can’t think past the tablets.
That’s completely understandable. You don’t need to decide anything today. Whatever you decide, I’ll support you.

Let me give you the honest picture. Babies exposed to valproate have around an 11 in 100 chance of a physical birth defect, such as a problem with the spine, face or heart. There’s also up to a 30 to 40 in 100 chance of problems with learning or development later. That also means many babies are not affected. The risk depends partly on the dose, and the specialists can look at your situation in detail.
model.why: Accurate MHRA figures, framed both ways

model.text: Thirty to forty… that’s so high.

It is significant, and I won’t pretend otherwise. That’s why I want the specialists involved quickly, not in weeks. They can review your medicine, plan detailed scans, and talk through all your options with you.
model.why: Acknowledges the figure and turns to action

model.text: What can I actually do right now?

Three things today. One, keep taking your valproate as prescribed. Two, I’ll prescribe folic acid 5 milligrams, a higher dose than usual, to take every day until at least 12 weeks. It helps most before pregnancy, but it’s still recommended now. Three, I’m making an urgent referral to the epilepsy specialist team and the pregnancy team today.
model.why: Clear three-part plan with honest framing of folic acid

model.text: Will they take me off it?
They may change it to a medicine that’s safer in pregnancy, but they’ll do it gradually and safely. That’s their decision with you, not something to do alone at home.
Okay.
Can I ask, gently, and not to blame you at all: had anyone talked with you before about valproate and pregnancy, or about contraception while on it?
model.why: Explores the Pregnancy Prevention Programme gap without blame

model.text: Can we come back to that? I can’t really think about it right now.
Of course. I’ll look at your records myself, and we can talk about it at your next appointment. It matters for your care, not for blame.
model.why: Respects her pace; commits to checking the record

model.text: While you’re waiting: showers rather than baths, and try to keep your sleep regular, because tiredness can trigger seizures. There’s also a national register for pregnant women with epilepsy that helps future mothers; the team can tell you about it.
model.why: Seizure-safety advice and the pregnancy register

model.text: If you have a seizure, call us or 111 the same day, and if a seizure lasts more than five minutes or they keep coming, whoever is with you should call 999. Also call if you have tummy pain or bleeding. What will you do when you put the phone down?
Keep taking the valproate, get the folic acid, wait for the specialists, and call if I have a seizure or any pain or bleeding.
Exactly right. I’ll ring you on Friday to make sure the appointment has come through, and to see how you’re feeling. You’re not on your own with this.
Thank you. I feel less panicky than when I rang.

social.t: Explore her feelings, support network and practical situation without assumption. Some women will want to continue; some will not. Both need timely, non-judgemental support.
Guilt and fear are common and can persist through pregnancy. Ask about mood at follow-up and in the antenatal period.

legal.t: If she chooses not to continue, women can self-refer to abortion services in England. A doctor with a conscientious objection must not obstruct access and must make sure she can see another doctor without delay (GMC).

Her seizures are controlled. If her medication is changed and a seizure follows, DVLA rules on medication-change seizures would apply; advise her to ask the specialists about driving during any switch.

professional.t: MHRA: all women who could become pregnant on valproate need the PPP, including effective contraception and an annual specialist review with the Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form. A pregnancy on valproate should prompt a practice review of her PPP status and, where there was a system failure, a significant event review.
Give accurate risk figures (GMC decision making and consent, 2020). If a gap in her previous care is found, be open with her about it.

community.t: The UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register (join while pregnant), Epilepsy Action, and the MHRA valproate patient guide. Community pharmacy should dispense valproate with the patient card and warning labels.

redFlags: Recent seizures or poor control (higher risk during any switch)
Abdominal pain or bleeding in early pregnancy (ectopic or miscarriage)
psychosocial: Her feelings about the pregnancy and her support
Guilt and fear driving the wish to stop the drug
Whether she had PPP counselling and contraception (asked without blame)
ice: Idea: valproate is dangerous, so she should stop it now
Concern: she has already harmed the baby; guilt
Expectation: to be told what to do today

playbook.diagnosis: “You’re about six weeks pregnant and valproate does carry real risks for the baby, so you need the specialists quickly. The safest thing today is to keep taking it, start high-dose folic acid, and let them plan any change with you.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of your valproate as the brakes on your seizures. Slamming the brakes off suddenly is dangerous. The specialists can change them over carefully, one set coming on as the other comes off.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if you’ve already harmed the baby, and you said you feel stupid. You haven’t done anything wrong. You called straight away, which is exactly right.”
management.psychosocial: Stay non-directive about the pregnancy; offer time and a follow-up call; return to the PPP question when she is ready; check mood at every contact.
sharedPlan: Continue valproate unchanged until specialist review
Folic acid 5 mg daily until at least 12 weeks
Urgent referral to the epilepsy specialist team and obstetric/maternal medicine team today
Seizure safety advice; information about the UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register
safetyNet: Same-day contact or 111 after any seizure; 999 if a seizure lasts over five minutes or seizures cluster
Call if abdominal pain or bleeding
Follow-up call on a set day to confirm the appointment

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you can hold two truths at once: valproate is a serious teratogen, and stopping it suddenly is dangerous. Candidates fail by picking one and ignoring the other, or by rushing past a frightened woman’s guilt.

items.fail: Advising her to stop valproate today.
items.why: Abrupt withdrawal risks seizures, status and SUDEP. MHRA and NICE NG217 both say not to stop without specialist advice.
items.fix: First sentence of your answer: “Please don’t stop it suddenly.” Then explain why.

items.fail: Vague risk: “there’s some risk to the baby.”
items.why: She is entitled to accurate figures (GMC decision making and consent). Vagueness sounds evasive.
items.fix: “Around 11 in 100 physical birth defects, up to 30–40 in 100 developmental problems. Many babies are not affected.”

items.fail: Referring routinely, or only to antenatal booking.
items.why: She needs urgent epilepsy specialist review and obstetric input. A routine referral may arrive after the window for decisions.
items.fix: “I’m making an urgent referral today to the epilepsy team and the pregnancy team, and I’ll check it has come through.”

items.fail: Asking “were you not using contraception?” early in the consultation.
items.why: Heard as blame; compounds guilt and shuts her down.
items.fix: Ask later, gently, and accept “can we come back to that?”.

items.fail: Assuming she wants to continue (or end) the pregnancy.
items.why: “Makes assumptions.” The pregnancy was unplanned and her feelings are unknown.
items.fix: “How do you feel about the pregnancy itself, separate from the tablets? You don’t have to decide today.”

items.fail: Ending with “the specialists will be in touch.”
items.why: Leaves a frightened woman alone with online fear, and no safety-net for seizures or early pregnancy problems.
items.fix: Three clear actions, named safety-net, teach-back, and a follow-up call on a set day.

timeMap.d: She asks whether to stop. Answer immediately: do not stop suddenly, and why.
Gestation, seizure control, other medicines and folic acid, pain or bleeding.
Address “what kind of mother” directly. Ask how she feels about the pregnancy, without assuming.
About 11% birth defects, up to 30–40% neurodevelopmental, dose-related. Frame both ways.
Continue valproate, folic acid 5 mg, urgent epilepsy and obstetric referral, PPP question gently, seizure safety, 999/111 advice, teach-back, call on a set day.

wordPics.fail: Tells her to stop valproate now, or reassures her the risk is small; no urgent referral; forgets folic acid; blames her for the pregnancy; assumes she will or won’t continue the pregnancy.
wordPics.pass: Leads with do-not-stop, gives the risk honestly, prescribes folic acid 5 mg, refers urgently to epilepsy and obstetric teams, and safety-nets for seizures.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: removes blame explicitly; asks how she feels about the pregnancy and stays non-directive; frames the figures both ways; honest that folic acid works best before conception; asks about the Pregnancy Prevention Programme gently and respects her pace; teach-back and a dated follow-up call.

avoid.dont: “Stop the valproate straight away to protect the baby.”
avoid.instead: “Please keep taking it for now. Stopping suddenly can cause seizures, which are dangerous for you both.”
avoid.why: Abrupt withdrawal is the most dangerous single piece of advice in this station.

avoid.dont: “Most babies are fine, so try not to worry.”
avoid.instead: “Around 11 in 100 have a physical birth defect and up to 30–40 in 100 have developmental problems. Many are not affected. The specialists will look at your situation.”
avoid.why: False reassurance breaches honest risk communication.

avoid.dont: “Weren’t you told to use contraception on this drug?”
avoid.instead: “Had anyone talked with you before about valproate and pregnancy? It matters for your care, not for blame.”
avoid.why: Blame compounds her guilt and shuts the conversation down.

Of course. I’ll look at your records myself, and we can talk about it at your next appointment. It matters for your care, not for blame.
SCA_MODELS.why: Respects her pace; commits to checking the record

SCA_MODELS.text: While you’re waiting: showers rather than baths, and try to keep your sleep regular, because tiredness can trigger seizures. There’s also a national register for pregnant women with epilepsy that helps future mothers; the team can tell you about it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Seizure-safety advice and the pregnancy register

SCA_MODELS.text: If you have a seizure, call us or 111 the same day, and if a seizure lasts more than five minutes or they keep coming, whoever is with you should call 999. Also call if you have tummy pain or bleeding. What will you do when you put the phone down?
Keep taking the valproate, get the folic acid, wait for the specialists, and call if I have a seizure or any pain or bleeding.
Exactly right. I’ll ring you on Friday to make sure the appointment has come through, and to see how you’re feeling. You’re not on your own with this.
Thank you. I feel less panicky than when I rang.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] MHRA National Patient Safety Alert NatPSA/2023/013/MHRA (November 2023) and MHRA Drug Safety Update (January 2024): valproate new safety measures · [2] MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2024): valproate use in men · [3] MHRA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme (Prevent) · [4] NICE NG217 (epilepsies, 2022, updated January 2025) · [5] NICE NG247 (maternal and child nutrition, 2025)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A woman on valproate with a positive pregnancy test needs three things today: do not stop the valproate suddenly, start folic acid 5 mg daily, and an urgent referral to the epilepsy specialist team and the obstetric team. Give honest risk information, respect her choices about the pregnancy, and find out why the Pregnancy Prevention Programme did not prevent this.

points.t: MHRA [1][2] and NICE NG217 [4]: patients should not stop valproate without specialist advice. Abrupt withdrawal risks convulsive seizures, status epilepticus, injury and SUDEP, all dangerous to mother and fetus. Any switch is planned and supervised by the specialist team.

MHRA [3]: children exposed to valproate in the womb have around an 11% risk of major birth defects (including neural tube defects, cleft lip and palate, heart and limb defects) and up to a 30–40% risk of neurodevelopmental disorders (learning difficulties, autism, ADHD). Risk rises with dose. Give these figures honestly and without catastrophising.

NICE NG217 [4]: refer women who are pregnant to the epilepsy specialist team for review of their anti-seizure medication, and share care with a specialist obstetric team and primary care. Make the referral urgently today. The specialists weigh switching against seizure risk and plan detailed anomaly scanning.

NICE NG247 [5]: offer folic acid 5 mg daily to those planning pregnancy or in the first 12 weeks who have an increased risk of a neural tube defect; NICE NG217 [4] recommends 5 mg daily for women on anti-seizure medication who could become pregnant. It works best before conception; start now anyway and continue to 12 weeks.

MHRA [1]: from 31 January 2024 valproate must not be started in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently document that there is no other effective or tolerated treatment. Women who could become pregnant must be on the Pregnancy Prevention Programme (effective contraception, pregnancy testing, annual specialist review with the Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form, now with a second specialist signature). MHRA [2] (September 2024): men taking valproate are advised to use effective contraception, as a precaution.

An unplanned pregnancy on a teratogenic drug raises choices she is entitled to make with full information: continuing the pregnancy with specialist care, or not continuing. The GP’s role is non-directive support and timely referral whichever she chooses.

Showers not baths, care with heights and cooking, sleep and stress management. Report any seizure promptly. Consultant-led antenatal care is needed; the UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register collects outcomes to inform future women and she can join while pregnant.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Noticed her distress and let her say it all; praised her for calling straight away.
Her feelings about the unplanned pregnancy, support, and emotional state, explored without assumptions.
Picked up “have I already harmed the baby” (guilt) and “should I stop it right now” (panic-stopping risk).
Her idea (valproate dangerous, maybe stop), concern (harm, guilt), expectation (what to do right now).
Gestation, seizure control, other medicines, folic acid, pain or bleeding; checked the record for PPP status.
Valproate exposure risk; seizure risk if stopped; early pregnancy complications.
Seizure-safety and status risk addressed; early pregnancy pain or bleeding screened.
Early unplanned pregnancy exposed to valproate: urgent specialist review needed; do not stop abruptly.
Continue valproate; folic acid 5 mg; urgent epilepsy and obstetric referral; non-directive support on her choices.
Pregnancy Prevention Programme gap explored without blame; mental health and support considered.
999/111 and same-day contact advice; teach-back; a booked follow-up call.

social.t: Explore her feelings, support network and practical situation without assumption. Some women will want to continue; some will not. Both need timely, non-judgemental support.
Guilt and fear are common and can persist through pregnancy. Ask about mood at follow-up and in the antenatal period.

legal.t: If she chooses not to continue, women can self-refer to abortion services in England. A doctor with a conscientious objection must not obstruct access and must make sure she can see another doctor without delay (GMC).

Her seizures are controlled. If her medication is changed and a seizure follows, DVLA rules on medication-change seizures would apply; advise her to ask the specialists about driving during any switch.

professional.t: MHRA: all women who could become pregnant on valproate need the PPP, including effective contraception and an annual specialist review with the Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form. A pregnancy on valproate should prompt a practice review of her PPP status and, where there was a system failure, a significant event review.
Give accurate risk figures (GMC decision making and consent, 2020). If a gap in her previous care is found, be open with her about it.

community.t: The UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register (join while pregnant), Epilepsy Action, and the MHRA valproate patient guide. Community pharmacy should dispense valproate with the patient card and warning labels.

redFlags: Recent seizures or poor control (higher risk during any switch)
Abdominal pain or bleeding in early pregnancy (ectopic or miscarriage)
psychosocial: Her feelings about the pregnancy and her support
Guilt and fear driving the wish to stop the drug
Whether she had PPP counselling and contraception (asked without blame)
ice: Idea: valproate is dangerous, so she should stop it now
Concern: she has already harmed the baby; guilt
Expectation: to be told what to do today

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “You’re about six weeks pregnant and valproate does carry real risks for the baby, so you need the specialists quickly. The safest thing today is to keep taking it, start high-dose folic acid, and let them plan any change with you.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of your valproate as the brakes on your seizures. Slamming the brakes off suddenly is dangerous. The specialists can change them over carefully, one set coming on as the other comes off.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if you’ve already harmed the baby, and you said you feel stupid. You haven’t done anything wrong. You called straight away, which is exactly right.”
management.psychosocial: Stay non-directive about the pregnancy; offer time and a follow-up call; return to the PPP question when she is ready; check mood at every contact.
sharedPlan: Continue valproate unchanged until specialist review
Folic acid 5 mg daily until at least 12 weeks
Urgent referral to the epilepsy specialist team and obstetric/maternal medicine team today
Seizure safety advice; information about the UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register
safetyNet: Same-day contact or 111 after any seizure; 999 if a seizure lasts over five minutes or seizures cluster
Call if abdominal pain or bleeding
Follow-up call on a set day to confirm the appointment

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you can hold two truths at once: valproate is a serious teratogen, and stopping it suddenly is dangerous. Candidates fail by picking one and ignoring the other, or by rushing past a frightened woman’s guilt.

items.fail: Advising her to stop valproate today.
items.why: Abrupt withdrawal risks seizures, status and SUDEP. MHRA and NICE NG217 both say not to stop without specialist advice.
items.fix: First sentence of your answer: “Please don’t stop it suddenly.” Then explain why.

items.fail: Vague risk: “there’s some risk to the baby.”
items.why: She is entitled to accurate figures (GMC decision making and consent). Vagueness sounds evasive.
items.fix: “Around 11 in 100 physical birth defects, up to 30–40 in 100 developmental problems. Many babies are not affected.”

items.fail: Referring routinely, or only to antenatal booking.
items.why: She needs urgent epilepsy specialist review and obstetric input. A routine referral may arrive after the window for decisions.
items.fix: “I’m making an urgent referral today to the epilepsy team and the pregnancy team, and I’ll check it has come through.”

items.fail: Asking “were you not using contraception?” early in the consultation.
items.why: Heard as blame; compounds guilt and shuts her down.
items.fix: Ask later, gently, and accept “can we come back to that?”.

items.fail: Assuming she wants to continue (or end) the pregnancy.
items.why: “Makes assumptions.” The pregnancy was unplanned and her feelings are unknown.
items.fix: “How do you feel about the pregnancy itself, separate from the tablets? You don’t have to decide today.”

items.fail: Ending with “the specialists will be in touch.”
items.why: Leaves a frightened woman alone with online fear, and no safety-net for seizures or early pregnancy problems.
items.fix: Three clear actions, named safety-net, teach-back, and a follow-up call on a set day.
